claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has fine, serrated grain boundaries.
Serrated grain boundaries distribute strain more evenly than straight grain boundaries.
Serrated grain boundaries maintain high ductility and toughness.
Combined high-temperature thermal cycling and mechanical loading induces a transition from serrated to straight grain boundaries.
A temperature near 650°C has been used in prior tensile and creep studies of a high-entropy alloy.
Brittle behavior in the proposed alloy arises from loss of grain-boundary serration rather than classical grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
Thermal activation permits local precipitate coarsening or atomic-species redistribution even in an initially single-phase alloy.
Precipitate coarsening or atomic redistribution destabilizes serrated boundaries and causes them to become straight.
Straight grain boundaries are less effective than serrated boundaries at distributing or arresting local strain concentrations.
Loss of boundary serration promotes localized stress and intergranular cracking.
Straight grain boundaries are associated with lower tensile fracture strain and shorter creep rupture life than serrated grain boundaries at elevated temperature.
Thermal-mechanical cycling will cause a marked reduction in ductility, toughness, and creep rupture life relative to the initial serrated-boundary baseline.
The proposed embrittlement is limited to high-temperature, high-strain service conditions.
At lower temperatures, the serrated morphology and associated toughness should persist.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis excludes intermetallic precipitation as the origin of brittleness, while the mechanism invokes precipitate coarsening as the event that destabilizes the beneficial boundary morphology.
The material is described as single-phase, but the mechanism assumes local precipitates capable of coarsening without specifying when or how a second phase forms.

The conditions state that grain-boundary morphology is the only variable, but the mechanism invokes precipitate and compositional redistribution, and the uncertainty field allows concurrent microstructural transformations.
